requirement:
# REQ-2129: Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2129

## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack
    
I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that will work for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.

For example:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

That's it. The class does not even need to declare a body (no `{` and `}`), because the actual implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as [`[IsExternalInit]`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/67687186/643085) or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using [`IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/docs/features/incremental-generators.md#outputting-values) instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

story.summary: Adds a public `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute (with an optional `SurrogateType` property) to MessagePack.Annotations. The source generator now finds partial classes carrying the attribute that implement exactly one `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`, and writes the formatter body into them. They are registered in `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`. With no surrogate, the type is serialized in contractless mode: public read-write members, string keys, ordered by name. With a surrogate, the surrogate type's `[Key]`/`[IgnoreMember]` attributes define the contract. Four new error diagnostics are added (MsgPack019–022), plus docs, a dependency-free test assembly, and execution and diagnostic tests.
story.why: REQ-2129 asks for a formatter for a type in a referenced assembly (Project A, which has no MessagePack reference) to be generated inside the consuming project (Project B) via an attribute on a partial formatter class.
touches_beyond_requirement: New public API in a shipped assembly: `GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute` with a `SurrogateType` property (static check S3 fails).
Four new user-visible analyzer rules, MsgPack019–MsgPack022, all Error severity (static check S4 fails).
A surrogate-type design for keys that is not one of the three alternatives listed in the issue.
Contractless string-key serialization chosen as the default wire contract for these formatters.
Both formatter T4 templates changed to emit `partial class` for user-declared formatters.
The custom-formatter discovery in GeneratorUtilities now skips attributed classes.
The MapMode execution test project excludes the new test files, so map mode is not exercised.
A new test project, MessagePack.SourceGenerator.ExternalTypes, targeting net8.0 only.
story.confidence_overview: High confidence in the happy path. Execution tests show contractless class/struct round-trips, the surrogate int-key layout, use inside a `[MessagePackObject]` type, and resolver registration. Diagnostic tests cover MsgPack019, 020, 021 (abstract only), 022 (name and type mismatch) and the MsgPack005 key mix. Untested paths: the missing-constructor diagnostic, generic or inaccessible data types, duplicate surrogate keys, surrogate string keys, the callback receiver, and map mode. The incremental pipeline carries Roslyn symbols in its values, which is a performance and correctness risk.

findings.description: GeneratedFormatterRequest holds INamedTypeSymbol values in an incremental pipeline. Symbols are not equatable across compilations, so the pipeline re-runs on every edit and keeps old compilations alive. The full collector also runs twice: once for the model and once for diagnostics at line 125.

Surrogate members come from GetInstanceMembers, which includes private and read-only fields and properties of the surrogate. Any explicitly declared private field or computed property on the surrogate without [Key] or [IgnoreMember] fails with MemberNeedsKey.

GetInstanceMembers keeps only the most-derived member of each name, including non-public ones. A private member in a derived class hides a public read-write base member of the same name, which is then silently not serialized in contractless mode.
NoDeserializingConstructor is created with no message arguments. If the existing descriptor's messageFormat has placeholders, the message is malformed. This path has no test.
If SurrogateType is set to a non-named type, such as an array, `as INamedTypeSymbol` yields null. The formatter then silently falls back to contractless mode with no diagnostic.

not_quoted: This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.
2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes.

This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as [`[IsExternalInit]`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/67687186/643085) or `[ModuleInitializer]`.

With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using [`IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/docs/features/incremental-generators.md#outputting-values) instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly.
This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency.
Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.
It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

The source generator now finds partial classes carrying the attribute that implement exactly one `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`, and writes the formatter body into them. They are registered in `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`. With no surrogate, the type is serialized in contractless mode: public read-write members, string keys, ordered by name. With a surrogate, the surrogate type's `[Key]`/`[IgnoreMember]` attributes define the contract.
